title: Help is strength
hookLine: depression and trauma are not spiritual failures, and professional help is part of the path

cards: The prophet Elijah is running for his life. He goes a day's journey into the wilderness, sits down under a juniper tree, and asks to die. In the King James Bible he says: "It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life."

Then he lies down and falls asleep. Some readers today hear in that scene something a doctor would take seriously: exhaustion, fear, despair, a person at the end of himself. And this is a prophet, a man of God.
What happens next is today's lesson.

teach.b: First, what the angel does. Not a sermon. The text says an angel touched him and said, "Arise and eat."

There's a cake baked on the coals and a jar of water by his head. He eats, drinks, sleeps again, and the angel comes back and feeds him a second time. Care for the body comes before any word about his calling.

teach.h: A HEALTH CONDITION, NOT A FAILURE.
teach.b: Depression, and the long shadow trauma can leave, are health conditions. Doctors, psychologists and counselors study them and treat them. They aren't proof of weak faith, a bad practice, or not trying hard enough.
Prayer, meditation and community can sit alongside treatment; they don't have to replace it. Third, the traditions have said something like this in their own words.
The book of Sirach, part of the Bible for Catholic and Orthodox Christians, tells its readers to honor the physician, because the Lord created him.

In a hadith collected by Abu Dawud, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells people to seek treatment, because God has not made a disease without making a remedy for it. Fourth, the strength part.
Elijah doesn't fix himself under that tree. Someone touches him, feeds him, lets him sleep, and he takes it.
Calling a doctor, a counselor, or a crisis line (988 in the US, call or text; anywhere else, your local emergency number) isn't a step off the path. For some people, it's the next step on it.

how: Some religious communities encourage people facing depression or trauma to see a doctor or counselor alongside prayer or meditation, and some congregations keep lists of local counselors and crisis lines.

o: a prophet fed and let sleep before any word of his calling
a prophet who never doubted or grew tired in his work
an angel who brought bread to people in the wilderness

games.q: help, from the texts — tap the pairs.

s: depression is a sign of weak faith
it's a health condition that doctors and counselors study and treat.
the angel's first help for Elijah is food, water and sleep
"arise and eat": a cake on the coals, a jar of water, and more sleep, twice.
the traditions in today's lesson say to avoid physicians and trust prayer alone
Sirach says to honor the physician, and a hadith in Abu Dawud says to seek treatment.

games.q: you're the angel. Elijah is asleep under the juniper tree, and he has just asked to die. what comes first?
o: a touch, food and water, and more sleep.
leave him to sort it out alone.
games.why: the angel touches him and says "arise and eat," then lets him sleep, and does it all again. care for the body comes first.

practice: Save one support number in your phone now: your doctor, a counselor, a crisis line where you live, or a friend who always picks up, under a plain name you'll find on a bad night.

Then put the phone down, breathe, and let your hands rest knowing it's there; if you pray, you can pray for the people who answer those phones. And if you're in danger right now, stop and call your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: Elijah, fed and let sleep by an angel under the juniper tree before any word about his calling. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: arise and eat. Even a prophet was fed before he was told anything. Day seven hundred thirty-eight, done.
